Research consistently shows it is more effective than placebo and equivalent to low-dose tricyclic antidepressants or standard selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for mild to moderate depression [d1][d3], and it has been described as a useful alternative to prescription antidepressants for mild depression [d3][d8]. However, evidence is mixed: some clinical studies show no additional benefit over placebo for moderately severe major depression [d2], and a peer-reviewed analysis notes it has comparable efficacy to SSRIs for mild-to-moderate depression but evidence is uncertain for severe depression, with limited long-term data [d5]. Overall, St. [d1] John's Wort appears to be a viable option for mild to moderate depression, though individuals with more severe symptoms should consider conventional treatment, and users should be monitored for potential drug interactions and side effects [d1][d5][d6].

Yes, iodine supplementation can cause thyroid problems, particularly when intake exceeds recommended levels. [d1] Research has shown that excess iodine can disrupt thyroid homeostasis and lead to both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, as well as autoimmune thyroiditis [d1][d3]. During pregnancy, maternal iodine supplementation has been associated with a 27.3% higher risk of elevated TSH levels in cord blood and an increased risk of TSH above 3 mIU/L in women consuming 200 µg or more daily [d2], highlighting a vulnerable population. Cardiac biomarkers are substances released into the blood when the heart is damaged or stressed, and are used to help diagnose acute coronary syndrome (ACS), myocardial infarction (heart attack), and heart failure [d1][d5].
